name: African Marigold
summary: A tender flowering annual with many garden cultivars. This species-level profile does not identify a particular flower color, series, or height class.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Tagetes erecta. NC State lists multiple cultivars with differing sizes and traits; this identity represents the species, not any named series.

growth.short: Tender flowering annual; cultivar sizes vary
growth.guidance: NC State reports garden forms spanning roughly 1–4 ft tall and 1–2 ft wide. Tall forms may need staking; do not treat those species-level ranges as dimensions for every cultivar.

cultivation.short: Full sun; evenly moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun for flowering, with light afternoon shade tolerated, and evenly moist, well-drained soil. Its outdoor guidance does not establish indoor hydroponic compatibility.

care.short: Pinch young plants; deadhead heavy spent flowers
care.guidance: NC State reports pinching young stems to encourage bushier growth and promptly removing spent heavy flower heads that could snap stems. Cultivar resistance to diseases varies.

flowering.short: Long summer-to-fall bloom; also grown as a cut flower
flowering.guidance: NC State describes fragrant, showy flower heads blooming from early summer into early fall, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds, and notes the species is popular in the cut-flower trade. Flower color, size and double form vary among cultivars; this source does not specify a home-garden cutting stage, and no color or form is assigned here.

safety.short: Sap may irritate skin, especially with sunlight exposure
safety.guidance: NC State reports that sap or juice contacting broken skin followed by sunlight can cause redness, burning and blisters; flower aroma may irritate the nose or eyes. This is source-reported low-severity hazard information, not a cultivar-specific claim.

problems.short: Disease and pest susceptibility varies by cultivar
problems.guidance: NC State lists possible botrytis, leaf spot, phytophthora, powdery mildew, rots, thrips, slugs and spider mites. Reported resistance differs among cultivars, so none is attributed to this unspecified identity.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor bedding culture does not establish compatibility with indoor nutrient-solution systems.

evidence.note: NC State describes the species as erect; cultivar form and size vary.

height.reason: NC State dimensions span cultivars; no cultivar is identified.

spread.reason: NC State dimensions span cultivars; no cultivar is identified.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor full-sun guidance is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Purple Coneflower
summary: A North American herbaceous perennial used in pollinator and native gardens. It is distinct from Echinacea pallida and the separately cataloged Tennessee coneflower.

identity.short: Accepted species; not a named coneflower cultivar
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Echinacea purpurea. NC State notes many cultivars with variable size, color and disease response; this record does not assign cultivar traits.

growth.short: Long-lived clumping perennial; regional sources report about 2–4 ft
growth.guidance: NC State reports 3–4 ft for the species in its garden context; Clemson gives 2–3.5 ft and Iowa State 1.5–3 ft. These are regional outdoor ranges, and cultivar size varies; they are not indoor-system estimates.

cultivation.short: Moist, well-drained soil; full sun to partial shade
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes adaptable soil tolerance, preference for moist well-drained loam, and full sun to partial shade in landscape use. This is not hydroponic compatibility evidence.

care.short: Deadhead selectively; retain some seed heads for wildlife
care.guidance: Iowa State reports that removing faded flowers can promote repeat bloom and reduce self-seeding; it also notes birds use the dried seed heads through winter. NC State recommends leaving some dead stems at 12–24 inches until they disintegrate for stem-nesting native bees, and Clemson notes winter seed heads attract goldfinches. Deadheading is therefore a choice based on bloom, reseeding and habitat goals, not an all-or-nothing rule.

propagation.short: Seed propagation is possible; household protocol unresolved here
propagation.guidance: NC State says the species is readily propagated by seed, but the selected species page does not specify germination conditions or a sowing protocol. Do not borrow a protocol from other Echinacea species.

flowering.short: A summer flush may continue at lower intensity until frost
flowering.guidance: Iowa State reports a large early-summer bloom flush followed by fewer flowers until first frost in its regional garden context. NC State describes summer into mid-fall flowering. Timing varies by region; fading flowers and later seed heads are normal lifecycle stages.

uses.short: Pollinator and wildlife perennial; stems also suit specialty cut flowers
uses.guidance: Clemson describes Echinacea as a specialty cut flower and a nectar source for butterflies; Iowa State also notes pollinator-garden use and winter seed value for birds. These genus-level or species-level landscape uses do not identify a cultivar or guarantee a cut-flower vase life.

problems.short: Japanese beetles, leaf spot and aster yellows may occur
problems.guidance: NC State lists Japanese beetles, leaf spot and susceptibility to aster yellows. Clemson also describes stem rots, powdery mildew, anthracnose, aphids and eriophyid mites in Echinacea, with symptoms often mild; it identifies witches'-broom, greened petals and stunting as aster-yellows signs and recommends removing infected plants. Phytophthora resistance is reported for some cultivars only and is not assigned to this species-level identity.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Native perennial landscape guidance does not establish indoor hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State describes erect stems and terminal flower heads.

height.reason: Outdoor mature dimensions are not an indoor-system size estimate.

spread.reason: No indoor pod footprint is documented.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Pale Purple Coneflower
summary: A distinct North American perennial coneflower. NC State documents seed handling that varies with stratification and fall or spring sowing.

identity.short: Accepted species; distinct from E. purpurea
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Echinacea pallida; NC State distinguishes it from purple coneflower by earlier flowering and narrower, hairier leaves. It is also distinct from E. tennesseensis.

growth.short: Upright perennial, about 2–3 ft in regional guidance
growth.guidance: NC State describes stout erect stems around 3 ft; Iowa State reports 2–3 ft tall by 1–1.5 ft wide in Iowa. The long taproot and outdoor measurements are not interpreted as indoor-system fit.

cultivation.short: Full sun and drained soil; part shade is tolerated regionally
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and well-drained soil. Iowa State describes E. pallida in full sun with dry-to-medium-dry soils and notes tolerance of poor soils and part shade in its regional context. The long taproot supports drought tolerance after establishment; these outdoor traits do not establish hydroponic compatibility.

care.guidance: NC State says clump division may be needed after several years; Iowa State likewise recommends dividing crowded clumps. The seed stratification and sowing instructions belong in the Seed Profile, not established-plant care.

propagation.guidance: NC State lists both seed and division. Its seed guidance is represented separately in Seed Profile; no cultivar is assigned.

flowering.short: Brief summer bloom; earlier than E. purpurea
flowering.guidance: NC State notes a short summer flowering period and earlier bloom than E. purpurea. Iowa State reports June–July bloom in its regional context and says plants may bloom freely without deadheading. Calendar timing is regional, not a fixed indoor schedule.

uses.short: Pollinator and wildlife perennial for dry-to-medium landscape sites
uses.guidance: Iowa State describes this species as a full-sun perennial for dry-to-medium soils that can tolerate part shade and spread by seed; it is included among garden coneflowers. NC State notes pollinators and birds use its flowers and seed heads. This is outdoor landscape context, not indoor suitability.

problems.short: Japanese beetles and leaf spot may occur
problems.guidance: NC State reports Japanese beetles and leaf spot. No disease-resistance claim is made for this species-level identity.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor perennial culture does not establish indoor nutrient-solution compatibility.

evidence.note: NC State describes stout erect stems.

height.reason: Landscape height is not an indoor-system height estimate.

spread.reason: An indoor footprint is not documented.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor full sun is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Moss Rose
summary: A low-growing, heat- and drought-tolerant ornamental succulent annual, distinct from common purslane (Portulaca oleracea). Institutional sources disagree about human food use, so Gardenpedia treats this identity as ornamental and does not recommend consumption; this is a cautious editorial policy, not a claim of human toxicity.

identity.short: Accepted ornamental species; no cultivar assigned
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Portulaca grandiflora. NC State explicitly distinguishes other plants also called purslane or moss rose, including P. oleracea; no named series is represented here.

growth.short: Prostrate mat-forming annual; about 8 in tall and 1 ft wide
growth.guidance: NC State reports a low mat-forming habit and these landscape dimensions. Flowers close overnight and in cloudy or rainy weather; no cultivar-specific flower form is claimed.

cultivation.short: Full sun and sharply drained sandy or rocky soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes heat and drought tolerance and recommends well-drained sandy or rocky soil in full sun. These conditions do not establish hydroponic suitability.

care.guidance: NC State reports that removing spent flowers deters self-seeding. It also notes that the species is low-maintenance; seedling handling and transplant sensitivity belong with seed-stage guidance, not this established-plant care section.

flowering.short: Flowers open in sun and close in cloudy or wet weather
flowering.guidance: NC State says the flowers close from sundown to sunrise and do not open on cloudy or rainy days. The low, spreading plant is used in rock or crevice gardens, border fronts, pots and hanging planters; flowering response is not a sign of plant failure in dim or wet weather.

uses.short: Ornamental use; Gardenpedia does not recommend consumption
uses.guidance: NC State's species profile lists P. grandiflora flowers and seeds as edible, and Wisconsin Extension says its seeds may be eaten raw or cooked. A 2026 UF/IFAS Charlotte County article says moss rose (P. grandiflora) is not edible and distinguishes it from edible common purslane (P. oleracea). Because these institutional sources conflict and no preparation guidance resolves the disagreement, Gardenpedia makes no food-use recommendation for this ornamental identity. This precaution does not establish human toxicity; the UF/IFAS pet-toxicity note is not generalized to people.

problems.short: Poor drainage may cause crown rot; aphids and slugs may occur
problems.guidance: NC State lists occasional aphids and slugs and crown rot in poorly drained soil.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Drought-adapted soil culture does not establish compatibility with nutrient solution.

evidence.note: NC State describes a low prostrate, spreading mat habit.

height.reason: Outdoor dimensions are not translated into a Garden X indoor-system estimate.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor full sun is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Indian Blanket Flower
summary: A species-level Gaillardia with showy two-toned heads and pollinator value. Sources describe it as annual or perennial; it is distinct from G. aristata and commercial interspecific hybrids.

identity.short: Accepted annual species; not a commercial hybrid
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Gaillardia pulchella. NC State notes other plants share the blanket-flower common name, including G. aristata and G. × grandiflora; this record is specifically G. pulchella.

growth.short: Erect annual or short-lived perennial; about 1.5–2 ft tall
growth.guidance: NC State describes an erect plant around 1.5–2 ft tall and about 1 ft wide in its regional garden context, flowering from summer into fall.

cultivation.short: Full sun to light shade; drained soil with even moisture
cultivation.guidance: For established plants, NC State recommends full sun while tolerating light shade, and garden soil that drains well and receives even moisture. It also reports heat, drought and salt tolerance in its regional outdoor context. Constant moisture for germination belongs to the Seed Profile, not mature-plant care; none of this establishes indoor hydroponic suitability.

care.short: Remove or retain seed heads according to reseeding goals
care.guidance: NC State notes seed heads support songbirds if left over winter. The species naturalizes; manage seed set according to local garden conditions.

flowering.short: Showy orange-red flowers from summer into fall
flowering.guidance: NC State describes a long summer-to-fall display whose nectar attracts butterflies. If seed heads remain over winter, songbirds use them. Flowering and seed-head retention are normal lifecycle/use information, not a disease signal.

uses.short: Useful in containers, borders, cutting gardens and naturalized meadows
uses.guidance: NC State lists containers, borders, cutting gardens, rock or cottage gardens, and naturalized meadows as landscape uses. It does not specify a home cutting stage or vase life, so none is inferred.

problems.short: Avoid waterlogged soil; aphids and thrips may occur
problems.guidance: NC State reports the species will not survive waterlogged soil and lists aphids and thrips as possible problems.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor border and container guidance does not establish indoor hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: NC State describes an erect flowering habit.

height.reason: Regional garden dimensions are not an indoor-system height estimate.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Great Blanket Flower
summary: A North American perennial wildflower distinct from annual Indian blanket flower (Gaillardia pulchella) and their commercial hybrids.

identity.short: Accepted perennial species; distinct from G. pulchella
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Gaillardia aristata. NC State notes that commercial G. × grandiflora is a hybrid of G. aristata and G. pulchella; this record does not represent that hybrid.

growth.short: Taprooted perennial; commonly 1–3 ft, potentially taller regionally
growth.guidance: NC State reports 1–3 ft tall by 1–2 ft wide. The University of Idaho Extension Western Native Plants guide describes Intermountain plants exceeding 3 ft with greater spread. These are regional landscape dimensions, not a cultivar-specific or indoor-system size estimate.

cultivation.short: Full sun preferred; avoid heavy, persistently wet soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and reports performance in hot, dry sites, with supplemental water during extended drought. The University of Idaho Extension regional guide says it tolerates moderately moist to dry conditions, blooms longer with supplemental water, and performs poorly in heavy, consistently wet soil. Its twice-monthly summer irrigation suggestion is regional, not a universal schedule. Neither source establishes indoor hydroponic suitability.

care.short: Remove dead foliage in spring; deadhead late-season flowers as desired
care.guidance: The University of Idaho Extension guide recommends removing dead foliage in spring, deadheading in late summer for appearance, and controlling volunteer seedlings where they are unwanted. NC State recommends gloves because the hairy surfaces may irritate skin and warns that overwatering or poor drainage can cause root rot.

propagation.short: Seed is preferred; division is also possible
propagation.guidance: The University of Idaho Extension guide says seed is the easiest propagation route and requires no stratification or other pretreatment; it also notes division and stem cuttings are possible. Seedling-stage handling and transplant readiness are detailed separately in the Seed Profile. NC State independently lists seed and division.

flowering.short: Long bloom; regional sources differ on the calendar window
flowering.guidance: NC State describes summer flowering. The University of Idaho Extension guide reports bloom from late spring through late fall in its Intermountain landscape context and May–October in its plant-list timing field. Treat bloom timing as regional rather than a universal calendar promise; flowers attract pollinators and seed heads attract birds.

uses.short: Native wildflower for mixed beds, borders and pollinator landscapes
uses.guidance: NC State and the University of Idaho Extension guide describe use in borders, cottage or rock gardens, wildflower meadows and pollinator gardens. The Western Native Plants guide also describes use in water-conserving landscapes. This is regional landscape guidance, not a universal drought-proof claim.

problems.short: Mildew, leaf spot, aster yellows and root rot can occur
problems.guidance: NC State lists powdery mildew, leaf spot, aster yellows and root rot under overwatering or poor drainage, and warns of reseeding. The University of Idaho Extension guide reports occasional powdery mildew that seldom needs control and says plants may become somewhat weedy in consistently moist conditions, while not considering them invasive. Manage volunteer seedlings where unwanted; do not interpret the regional observation as disease resistance.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Native perennial landscape use does not establish compatibility with indoor nutrient-solution systems.

evidence.note: NC State describes erect stems and a clumping/mounding form.

height.reason: Outdoor dimensions are not used as an indoor-system estimate.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor full sun is not an indoor grow-light tier.
